report: The patient fell with an e-cigarette in his mouth, then developed stridor and respiratory distress. Examination showed diffuse supraglottic edema; CT revealed glottic and supraglottic swelling without fracture; direct laryngoscopy showed mucosal sloughing most severe in the epiglottis. This pattern is characteristic of thermal/chemical injury from e-cigarette aspiration. The absence of laryngeal fracture reduces the likelihood of traumatic laryngeal injury, while the lack of allergic trigger and the trauma context make angioedema and infectious supraglottitis less likely. Therefore the evidence converges on e-cigarette airway injury as the most probable diagnosis.
answer: Chemical burns of the pharynx and esophagus due to e-cigarette injury
